images.alt: A DEC PDP-11/34 minicomputer cabinet on display in a computer museum
images.caption: A PDP-11/34 — one of the many cabinet sizes DEC built around the same 16-bit architecture between 1970 and 1997.

images.alt: Close-up of a PDP-11/34 front panel showing its octal keypad and row of LED indicator lights
images.caption: The front panel's switches and lamps are the machine's own address and data display — no PDP-11 came without one.

images.commonsFile: File:DEC PDP-11-40 Minicomputer, 1973, Technisches Museum Wien (edited, white background).jpg
images.alt: A DEC PDP-11/40 minicomputer cabinet, 1973, photographed against a plain white background
images.caption: A PDP-11/40, 1973 — one of the many DEC-built variants that ran RT-11, RSX-11M, or RSTS/E depending on what the customer bought.

images.alt: A DEC VT100 video display terminal with keyboard, the kind commonly attached to a PDP-11
images.caption: A terminal like this is how most people met a PDP-11: not the cabinet, but a keyboard and a screen at the end of a serial line.

images.alt: A DEC RL02 removable disk data cartridge, the kind used to boot and store data on PDP-11 systems
images.caption: An RL02 cartridge — the removable disk pack that held RT-11, RSX-11M, and RSTS/E on real PDP-11 hardware.
